The narrator has deliberately killed his own sibling. To conceal the murder, he is trying to fake a farewell note in the sibling's handwriting, so it will appear the sibling was deeply disappointed with someone and voluntarily left forever ("I'm never coming back"). He practices forging the sibling's handwriting by writing that farewell sentence over and over—the seven identical lines are his repeated practice drafts. When he looks at the pile of practice sheets, he sighs: those sheets are themselves incriminating evidence of the forgery, so he realizes he is in serious trouble—the very act of practicing the note has left a trail proving the farewell is fake.

The narrator has deliberately killed his own sibling. To conceal the killing, he wants it to appear the sibling left of their own accord—never coming back—so he practices forging the sibling's handwriting by writing a farewell sentence seven times. The seven identical lines are his successive practice drafts of that forged note. The "Sigh, I know I'm in trouble" is the narrator's realization that the practice sheets themselves are incriminating: they are written in his hand and prove he was fabricating the sibling's goodbye, so his cover story is already exposed and he will be caught.
